claims.text: A hybrid DFT and machine-learning approach can predict melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties of high-entropy alloys with less than 5% error relative to experiment.
The proposed input materials are solid high-entropy alloys with well-characterized multicomponent compositions.
Systematic DFT calculations on a representative subset of high-entropy alloys can provide electronic-structure and interatomic-bonding descriptors.
Machine-learning models trained on DFT-derived descriptors can interpolate melting-related thermodynamic properties across high-entropy-alloy composition space.
Validation experiments should be conducted under equilibrium conditions with controlled, uniform heating at ambient and high pressures.
Local bonding environments, density of states, and interatomic potential energies mediate the relationship between alloy composition and melting properties.
Calculated electronic and atomic descriptors correlate with macroscopic thermodynamic behavior at melting.
Machine-learning models can capture complex nonlinear interactions in the high-dimensional compositional space of high-entropy alloys.
Learning these nonlinear interactions allows predictions to be extended efficiently to regimes not explicitly calculated by DFT.
The integrated method will predict melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change at melting with less than 5% error.
The integrated method will accurately predict liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
Methods relying solely on direct calorimetry and exhaustive first-principles calculations are less efficient than the proposed hybrid approach.
Conventional methods typically have prediction errors greater than 10%.
Compositional inhomogeneity or phase separation near melting may reduce the applicability of the approach.
Under conditions involving inhomogeneity or phase separation, DFT accuracy may decline and the ML training set may be insufficient.
Extensive experimental data are lacking across the full high-entropy-alloy compositional space.
Approximations inherent in DFT and ML create uncertainty in the generalizability of the proposed method.
High-resolution calorimetry, in situ X-ray diffraction, and complementary thermodynamic measurements can be used to compare predictions against experimental values.
An average prediction error above 5% across the tested alloys would falsify the hypothesis.
Systematic failure for a subset of compositions would falsify the hypothesis by indicating a breakdown in ML generalizability or DFT accuracy.
